title: Already, now, will
goal: Mark time with three separate little words for *already*, *in progress* and *will* — without a single verb changing its form.
bekal: use *đã*, *đang*, *sẽ* and know when all three can be dropped
tell *rồi* at the end of a sentence apart from *đã* before the verb
ask with *… chưa?* and answer with *Rồi* or *Chưa*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Gọi điện cho chị Linh
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon. Budi calls Linh. Notice how each refers to themselves — Linh uses *chị*, Budi uses *em*, exactly as in the rule from Unit 1.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Chị Linh à? Budi đây. Chị đang làm gì đấy?
lines.id: Linh? It's Budi. What are you up to?
lines.literal: older-sister Linh huh? Budi here. older-sister in-progress do what there?
lines.baca: Chị Ling à? Budi dây. Chị dang làm gì dấy?

lines.speaker: Linh:
lines.text: Chị đang nấu cơm. Em ăn cơm chưa?
lines.id: I'm cooking. Have you eaten yet?
lines.literal: older-sister in-progress cook rice. younger-sibling eat rice not-yet?
lines.baca: Chị dang nấu kơm. Em ăn kơm chưa?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Em ăn rồi ạ. Lúc nãy em đã ăn phở ở quán gần nhà.
lines.id: I've eaten. Earlier I had phở at a place near home.
lines.literal: younger-sibling eat already (polite). moment earlier younger-sibling did eat phở at shop near house.
lines.baca: Em ăn zồi ạ. Lúk nãy em dã ăn fở ở kwán gần nyà.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ngon lắm! Chiều nay chị có rảnh không ạ?
lines.id: Really good! Are you free this afternoon?
lines.literal: tasty very! afternoon this older-sister have free not (polite)?
lines.baca: Ngon lắm! Chiều nay chị kó zảng không ạ?

lines.speaker: Linh:
lines.text: Chiều nay chị bận. Nhưng tối chị sẽ đi uống cà phê.
lines.id: I'm busy this afternoon. But tonight I'm going out for coffee.
lines.literal: afternoon this older-sister busy. but evening older-sister will go drink coffee.
lines.baca: Chiều nay chị bận. Nyưng tối chị sẽ di uống kà fê.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Em đi với chị được không ạ?
lines.literal: younger-sibling go with older-sister can not (polite)?
lines.baca: Em di với chị dượk không ạ?

lines.speaker: Linh:
lines.text: Được chứ! Em đã đến quán Cộng bao giờ chưa?
lines.id: Of course! Have you ever been to Cộng café?
lines.literal: can of-course! younger-sibling did come shop Cộng when not-yet?
lines.baca: Dượk chứ! Em dã dến kwán Kộng bao zờ chưa?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Chưa ạ. Em vẫn chưa đi bao giờ.
lines.id: No, never. I still haven't been.
lines.literal: not-yet (polite). younger-sibling still not-yet go ever.
lines.baca: Chưa ạ. Em vẫn chưa di bao zờ.

lines.speaker: Linh:
lines.text: Thế thì tối nay đi nhé. Bảy giờ, chị sắp xong việc rồi.
lines.id: Then let's go tonight. Seven o'clock — I'm almost done with work.
lines.literal: so then evening this go OK. seven hour, older-sister about-to finish work already.
lines.baca: Thế thì tối nay di nyé. Bảy zờ, chị sắp song việk zồi.

notes: **The verb doesn't change at all.** *Ăn* is still *ăn* for yesterday, now and tomorrow. Only the little word in front changes — and even that can be dropped when the time is clear from the sentence. "Yesterday I eat there" is perfectly good Vietnamese.

**Rồi at the end of a sentence is used more than đã in front.** *Em ăn rồi* is the most natural way to say "I've eaten". *Đã* is used when you want to stress that the action is really in the past, often with a past time word: *lúc nãy em đã ăn phở*.

**Đấy at the end of a question softens it.** *Chị đang làm gì đấy?* feels like "what're you up to, then?" — friendly and light. Without *đấy* the question sounds more demanding. You'll meet this little word many times before it's fully dissected in Unit 17.

**Bao giờ chưa? means "have you ever …?"** — literally "when, not yet?". The pattern: verb + *bao giờ chưa?* The answer is *Rồi* (yes, I have) or *Chưa* (not yet). To say "never", use *chưa … bao giờ*: *Em chưa đi bao giờ.*

**Sắp means "about to", and often pairs with rồi at the end**: *chị sắp xong rồi* = "I'm almost done". The pair looks like a clash — "about to" meets "already" — but it feels just like English "I'm nearly done now".

**Ạ at the end of a sentence is a mark of respect toward someone older**, and Budi uses it on almost every line because Linh is older. It has no meaning of its own and can't be translated — it just raises the politeness by one notch, a bit like adding "sir" or "ma'am". Dropping it with someone much older sounds cold.

grammars.title: Three time markers — and what they match
body: This is the most relieving part of Vietnamese for English speakers. No past tense, no future tense, no irregular verbs. There are three words, placed before the verb, and each one matches an English idea directly.
after: ⚠️ **All three can be dropped when the time is already clear.** *Hôm qua tôi ăn phở* ("yesterday I eat phở") is complete without *đã* — *hôm qua* already gives the time. English, by contrast, **must** use the past tense even when "yesterday" is right there.
So don't sprinkle *đã* over every past sentence. Beginners often do, and it sounds heavy, like someone saying "yesterday I did eat, did go, did come home".

grammars.title: Asking "… yet?"
body: One frame, and one of the ones you'll hear most in Vietnam — including as a casual greeting.

head: Question
Meaning
Answer: yes
Answer: not yet
rows: Have you ever been to Huế?

after: ⚠️ **Don't answer a *chưa?* question with *không*.** *Không* means "no, and I won't" — it closes the door. *Chưa* means "not yet, but maybe later". Answering *Anh ăn cơm chưa?* with *Không* sounds like you refuse to eat at all.
*Xong* means "finished" and is very often used alone: *Xong chưa?* — *Xong rồi!* Two two-word sentences you'll use every day, in class and at the food stall.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern: **trước** = before/last, **sau** = after/next. Once you hold those two words, most rows in this table needn't be memorized one by one. The only exceptions are *hôm qua*, *ngày mai* and *năm ngoái* — three frozen words to learn as they are.
⚠️ *Hôm nay* (today) uses *hôm*, but *ngày mai* (tomorrow) uses *ngày*. Both mean "day"; *hôm* is the day as lived, *ngày* the day as a unit. At A1, just learn each pair whole.

blocks.title: The best news in this whole course
items: Every verb in that table **will never change its form**, for as long as you use Vietnamese. Not for the person, not for the time, not for number. What you see in that column is the only form there is.

Compare French, where one verb can have more than thirty forms — or English, with its *go / went / gone* and *eat / ate / eaten*. The months learners of European languages spend memorizing irregular verbs, you can spend entirely on practicing tones. That's a very good trade.
Bây giờ tôi ____ ăn cơm. (in progress)
Hôm qua tôi ____ đi Hà Nội. (already)

exercises.prompt: Answer twice — once *Rồi*, once *Chưa* — in full. Separate them with a slash.
items: Anh đi Huế bao giờ chưa?
Anh gọi điện cho chị Linh chưa?

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: đi / sẽ / tối / uống / cà phê / tôi
nãy / lúc / phở / tôi / ăn / đã

answers: Ăn rồi. / Chưa ăn. — Rồi. / Chưa bao giờ. — Xong rồi. / Chưa xong. — Rồi. / Chưa. — Gọi rồi. / Chưa gọi.
Tôi đang nấu cơm. — Hôm qua tôi ăn phở. — Tối nay tôi sẽ uống cà phê. — Tôi chưa đi Huế bao giờ. — Tôi sắp xong rồi. — Tôi mới dậy.
Anh ăn cơm chưa? — Chiều nay chị bận. — Tối tôi sẽ đi uống cà phê. — Lúc nãy tôi đã ăn phở. — Tôi xong rồi.
